title: Same and different: comparing two things

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 26 Nov 2026 against DfE Development Matters (2021): Characteristics of Effective Learning, 'Creating and thinking critically: making links and noticing patterns in their experience'; Reception Understanding the World 'compare and contrast characters from stories'; and the EYFS Statutory Framework (2024) ELGs Past and Present, People, Culture and Communities and The Natural World, which each ask children to 'know some similarities and differences'. Every comparison fact was checked: cats and horses both have four legs and fur, cats miaow and horses neigh; ducks have feathers, wings and webbed feet, fish have fins and scales, both swim and have eyes; strawberries and fire engines are red; a football and an orange are both round; penguins have wings but cannot fly (they use them as flippers to swim). The lab's houses are drawn so that exactly one part differs in each round (chimney, right window, door handle), verified on screenshots.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented young-child comparison errors: judging on a global glance rather than feature by feature (Gentner 2010; Gentner and Namy 1999 show side-by-side alignment is what lets children notice shared structure) in the step 1 prediction 'different in every way' and the 'whole' slip; over-generalising same to mean identical (step 4 prediction 'not in any way' and the 'all' slip: red sock and red hat); confusing the contrast word but with both (step 2 prediction and WORD_NO messages, the 'word' slip); placing a shared feature on one side (step 3 prediction 'only the fish, because fish swim', the 'zone' slip); and stopping at salient differences so a small one is missed (step 5 door handle, the 'big' slip).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is structured comparison of a pair shown side by side: a feature-by-feature Same/Different judgement that builds a running comparison table, a sentence gap that only accepts both for a shared feature and but for a contrast, a three-box only-this / both / only-that sort (a Venn layout with the shared box in the middle), a pick-the-shared-dimension task for unlike pairs, and a part-by-part check of two drawn houses where each tapped part is ringed as checked. It is not flagsort (sorting many toys by one rule), the noticing-changes lab (one thing before and after), flagbecause or any spot-the-pattern lab, and it could not be relabelled for another topic because every task is about aligning two things' features.

lab_teaches.evidence: Children discover the key idea by doing it: the cat and horse turn out to share legs and fur though they look different, the duck and fish both swim, the strawberry matches the fire engine only in colour, and the tiny door handle is found only by checking each part. Each step's done message then names what they found ('same legs and fur, but a different size and sound'), and the kid text confirms the rule afterwards.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'different in every way' (disproved when legs and fur match), 'but' as the same-word (the gap rejects but for 'are round'), 'only the fish, because fish swim' (the card bounces with 'Ducks can swim too!'), and 'not the same in any way' for a strawberry and a fire engine (both are red). The reveal line names the prediction afterwards.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions; each wrong option carries a slip tag with its own message: 'whole' (a quick look misses things, check one part at a time), 'all' (same in one way is not the same in every way: the same what?), 'word' (both tells same, but tells different), 'zone' (if both can do it, it goes in the middle) and 'big' (differences can be tiny, check every part). Lab steps also give item-specific feedback, e.g. 'Count the legs. The cat has 4 and the horse has 4.'

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and words a 4-year-old hears daily (same, different, both, but, check); validate_lessons.py passes the kid (6.5) and adult (9.5) limits. Lab prompts are one short instruction each, with pictures for every thing compared and big tiles (the fig has the young class).

no_filler.evidence: Every sentence either teaches a part of comparing (one part at a time, both, but, three-way sort, same-what, small differences) or checks it. No filler phrases (content gate passed), no template text shared with other lessons (explanation under the 12% similarity limit).

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at iPhone 13 (390 px) in light and dark themes for every step before and after Show me: the pair pictures, Same/Different tiles, both/but tiles, three sort boxes with two-column cards, and both houses fit with nothing clipped; the final spot-the-difference line was wrapped after an earlier screenshot showed it clipped. A real drag of 'Can swim' onto 'Only the fish' was tested and gives the red feedback.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label ('Legs: the same', 'Put both in the gap', 'Can swim goes in Both', 'They are the same because: Same colour', 'Check the chimney on the right house'), so dragging and tapping the canvas are optional. The canvas aria-label updates with every result, challenge feedback is a polite live region, and the browser gate ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no violations or console errors.

sources: DfE (2021) Development Matters: non-statutory curriculum guidance for the early years foundation stage, Characteristics of Effective Learning and Understanding the World (Reception)
DfE (2024) Statutory framework for the early years foundation stage, ELGs Past and Present; People, Culture and Communities; The Natural World
Gentner, D. (2010) Bootstrapping the mind: analogical processes and symbol systems. Cognitive Science 34(5), 752-775
Gentner, D. and Namy, L. L. (1999) Comparison in the development of categories. Cognitive Development 14(4), 487-513
